title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Um wie viel Uhr? — Um halb neun

rules.text: THE VERB IS SECOND in a German main clause, and "second" counts PHRASES, not words. Ich gehe am Samstag ins Kino and Am Samstag gehe ich ins Kino are both ordinary — front the time and the subject moves behind the verb — while Am Samstag ich gehe is not German at all. English fronts a time and changes nothing, which is why this is the module's grammar and not a footnote.

The companion rule, and it is one line: when a time and a place both appear, TIME COMES FIRST. Am Donnerstag fahre ich nach Berlin, never the other way round. English prefers the reverse order and nobody ever says so out loud.

halb neun IS HALF PAST EIGHT. German counts toward the hour that is coming, where English counts back from the one that has gone: halb acht is 7:30, halb neun is 8:30, halb zehn is 9:30. There is no rule to learn beyond the direction of the counting, and this is the single mistake in the course most likely to make a learner miss a train. Viertel nach and Viertel vor behave exactly like English and are not the problem.

Plans are made among friends, so this module speaks du and wir and chips informal where the frame is du-only. M4 and M7 speak Sie and this one deliberately does not: an invitation in Sie reads as a business appointment. The suggestion frame is M1's modal bracket with wir — Wollen wir ins Kino gehen? Sollen wir um acht essen? — so no new structure is opened and the budget goes to the clock and the word order.

der Morgen ("the morning"), morgen ("tomorrow") and morgens ("in the mornings") are one index key and two relatives of it, because the fold cannot see the capital. L1-M6's morgen owns the key and everything here lands on it; the sentence around it is what tells a reader which one is meant.

sentences.cue: Shall we go to the cinema?

words.note: With wir in front it is not "do we want" but "shall we" — the ordinary German invitation. The infinitive gehen waits at the very end, which is M1's bracket again.
Its verb form is spelled exactly like the infinitive — wir gehen, wir wollen — so wir costs the index nothing new, the same bargain Sie struck in L1.

sentences.trap: Wollen wir …? is an INVITATION, not a question about desire. A learner translating it as "do we want to" will hear a strange sentence where a German hears the most normal offer there is.
sentences.sound: VOLL-en veer ins KEE-no GAY-en. The w of wollen and wir is a v.

variations.cue: Shall we go out to eat?
variations.changed: two infinitives, both at the end

variations.cue: Should we go to the cinema?
variations.changed: sollen, which asks for a decision rather than offers

variations.display: Wollen wir am Samstag ins Kino gehen?
variations.cue: Shall we go to the cinema on Saturday?
variations.changed: with a day inside the bracket

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end: Wollen wir ins Kino gehen?

sentences.usage: Suggesting something to a friend — the default invitation.
sentences.mnemonic: Wollen wir opens the offer. The infinitive closes it.

words.note: Literally mid-week, and it is the only German day without a -tag on the end. Every day is masculine, so it is am Mittwoch with L1-M4's am.

sentences.trap: German asks whether you HAVE time, not whether you are free. Bist du frei? is a question about being unattached or off work, and asking it about Wednesday evening will get you an odd look.
sentences.sound: hast doo am MITT-vokh tsite. Zeit begins with a ts and rhymes with English "kite".

variations.cue: Are you free on Sunday?
variations.changed: a different day

variations.cue: Are you free on Wednesday?
variations.changed: to someone you address as Sie

variations.cue: Are you free tomorrow?
variations.changed: tomorrow, which takes no am at all

mistake.why: Time is something you have: Hast du am Mittwoch Zeit?

sentences.usage: Opening a plan — asked before anything is proposed.
sentences.mnemonic: You HAVE time in German. You are not free.

sentences.display: Um wie viel Uhr treffen wir uns?
sentences.literal: At how much clock meet we us?

words.note: Um wie viel Uhr is the fixed way to ask a time — literally "at how much o'clock". It is three words and none of them can be dropped.
Meeting is reflexive in German: wir treffen UNS, literally "we meet us". Leave the uns out and the sentence is waiting for an object that never comes.

sentences.trap: sich treffen needs its pronoun. Wir treffen um acht is not a shorter way of saying it — it is an unfinished sentence, and the uns is what finishes it.
sentences.sound: oom vee feel oor TREFF-en veer oons. viel is said feel, with an f.

variations.cue: When shall we meet?
variations.changed: wann, which asks about the day as well

variations.display: Um wie viel Uhr gehen wir?
variations.cue: What time are we going?
variations.changed: a verb that needs no uns

variations.cue: Where shall we meet?
variations.changed: the place instead of the time

mistake.display: Um wie viel Uhr treffen wir?
mistake.why: Meeting is reflexive: Um wie viel Uhr treffen wir uns?

sentences.usage: The second thing asked, once the day is agreed.
sentences.mnemonic: We meet US. The uns is not optional.

words.note: halb neun is 8:30, NOT 9:30. German is halfway TO nine where English is half past eight. The number you say is the hour ahead of you, not the one behind.
L1-M8 counted to eight for prices; the clock needs the rest. zehn beside it, so halb zehn is half past nine.

sentences.trap: This is the mistake that makes people miss trains. halb neun said by a German means 20:30, and an English speaker who hears "half nine" and arrives at 21:30 has waited an hour alone.
sentences.sound: oom halp noyn. The b of halb is said as a p, and eu and äu are both said oy.

variations.cue: At half past seven
variations.changed: an hour earlier — the number still runs ahead

variations.cue: At half past nine
variations.changed: an hour later

variations.cue: At nine
variations.changed: the hour itself, where the counting question does not arise

mistake.display: Um halb neun, also um neun Uhr dreißig
mistake.why: halb neun is 8:30: um halb neun, also um acht Uhr dreißig.

sentences.usage: Settling a time — and the one to repeat back in digits if it matters.
sentences.mnemonic: halb runs AHEAD. halb neun is 8:30.

sentences.display: Am Samstag gehe ich ins Kino
sentences.cue: On Saturday I'm going to the cinema
sentences.literal: On-the Saturday go I into-the cinema

words.note: Samstag in the south and west and increasingly everywhere; Sonnabend is the northern and eastern word and is worth recognising rather than saying.

sentences.trap: The time is first and so the SUBJECT moves behind the verb. Am Samstag ich gehe is the sentence an English speaker builds, and it is not German — the verb holds the second slot no matter what stands in the first.
sentences.sound: am ZAMS-tahk GAY-uh ikh ins KEE-no. The s at the start of Samstag is a z.

variations.display: Ich gehe am Samstag ins Kino
variations.cue: I'm going to the cinema on Saturday
variations.changed: the ordinary order — same meaning, no fronting

variations.display: Am Sonntag gehe ich ins Kino
variations.cue: On Sunday I'm going to the cinema
variations.changed: a different day, same shape

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to the cinema
variations.changed: with L1-M6's morgen in the first slot

mistake.display: Am Samstag ich gehe ins Kino
mistake.why: The verb holds second place: Am Samstag gehe ich ins Kino.

sentences.usage: Announcing a plan, with the day as the point of the sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: Whatever comes first, the verb comes second.

words.note: sollen asks someone else to DECIDE, where wollen offers. Sollen wir …? hands the choice over; Wollen wir …? puts one on the table.

sentences.trap: sollen is not "should" in the advice sense. Du sollst is close to an instruction from somebody else, and Ich soll arbeiten means I have been told to, not that it would be wise.
sentences.sound: ZOLL-en veer oom acht ESS-en. The ch of acht is the back sound, scraped rather than said.

variations.cue: Shall we eat at eight?
variations.changed: an offer rather than a question about the decision

variations.display: Sollen wir um halb neun essen?
variations.cue: Shall we eat at half past eight?
variations.changed: with the counting-ahead half hour

variations.cue: Shall we go to the cinema?
variations.changed: a different plan, same frame

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end: Sollen wir um acht essen?

sentences.usage: Handing a decision to the other person, politely.
sentences.mnemonic: wollen offers. sollen asks you to decide.

sentences.display: Wir treffen uns um Viertel nach acht
sentences.cue: We're meeting at a quarter past eight
sentences.literal: We meet us at quarter after eight

words.note: Viertel nach and Viertel vor behave exactly like English, and only halb runs ahead. nach is M4's row doing the clock's "past", and vor is L1-M7's doing its "to".

sentences.trap: Only halb counts forward. A learner who has been burned by halb neun and then guesses that Viertel nach acht must be 7:45 has over-corrected — the quarters are the easy ones.
sentences.sound: veer TREFF-en oons oom FEER-tel nakh acht. Viertel starts with an f.

variations.display: Wir treffen uns um Viertel vor neun
variations.cue: We're meeting at a quarter to nine
variations.changed: vor, which is "to" on a clock

variations.display: Wir treffen uns um halb neun
variations.cue: We're meeting at half past eight
variations.changed: the half hour, which does count ahead

variations.display: Treffen wir uns um Viertel nach acht?
variations.cue: Shall we meet at a quarter past eight?
variations.changed: as a question, with the verb in front

mistake.display: Wir treffen uns um Viertel nach halb neun
mistake.why: A quarter past eight is Viertel nach acht.

sentences.usage: Confirming a time that is not on the hour.
sentences.mnemonic: The quarters behave. Only halb runs ahead.

words.note: The shops are shut and this is a fact about the day, not a preference. It is why Sonntag turns up in every plan a German makes for the weekend.
frei haben is time off work. It is not the frei of "free of charge", which is kostenlos, and not the free of Hast du Zeit?

sentences.trap: frei haben is about work and nothing else. Ist der Platz frei? asks whether a seat is taken, and neither of them will answer whether somebody is available this evening — that question is Hast du Zeit?
sentences.sound: am ZONN-tahk HAH-buh ikh fry. frei rhymes with English "fry".

variations.cue: I'm off on Saturday
variations.changed: a different day

variations.cue: I'm off on Sunday
variations.changed: the ordinary order, with no fronting

variations.display: Am Sonntag habe ich keine Zeit
variations.cue: I have no time on Sunday
variations.changed: the other answer, with L1-M3's kein

mistake.why: Time off is something you have: Am Sonntag habe ich frei.

sentences.usage: Answering an invitation before a time is proposed.
sentences.mnemonic: You HAVE time off, not are it.

sentences.display: Am Donnerstag fahre ich nach Berlin
sentences.cue: On Thursday I'm going to Berlin
sentences.literal: On-the Thursday travel I to Berlin

words.note: Thunder's day — the same god behind English Thursday, which makes it the easiest German day to keep. Donner is thunder and is worth hearing inside it.

sentences.trap: TIME comes before PLACE in German, which is the reverse of the English habit. Ich fahre nach Berlin am Donnerstag is understandable and is not what a German says.
sentences.sound: am DONN-ers-tahk FAH-ruh ikh nakh ber-LEEN. Berlin takes its stress on the second syllable.

variations.display: Ich fahre am Donnerstag nach Berlin
variations.cue: I'm going to Berlin on Thursday
variations.changed: no fronting, and the time is still before the place

variations.display: Am Mittwoch fahre ich nach Berlin
variations.cue: On Wednesday I'm going to Berlin
variations.changed: a different day

variations.display: Am Donnerstag fahre ich mit dem Zug
variations.cue: On Thursday I'm going by train
variations.changed: M4's mit + dative instead of a destination

mistake.display: Ich fahre nach Berlin am Donnerstag
mistake.why: Time comes before place: Ich fahre am Donnerstag nach Berlin.

sentences.usage: Saying where you will be, when the day is what matters.
sentences.mnemonic: Time, then place. Always that way round.

words.note: One word closes a plan in German, and it is warmer than it looks — abgemacht between friends is a handshake, not a contract.
bis Freitag, bis morgen, bis später: bis plus when is the whole goodbye. It says the meeting is settled, so it is never said to a stranger.

sentences.trap: bis Freitag is a farewell and it PROMISES the meeting. Say it to somebody you might see on Friday and they will expect you; Auf Wiedersehen is the goodbye with nothing attached.
sentences.sound: AP-guh-macht, biss FRY-tahk. The b of ab is said as a p.

variations.cue: Agreed — see you Saturday
variations.changed: a different day

variations.cue: Agreed — see you tomorrow
variations.changed: with L1-M6's morgen

variations.cue: Good — see you Friday
variations.changed: a plainer close

mistake.why: The farewell takes bis: Abgemacht, bis Freitag.

sentences.usage: Ending the conversation once the day and time are fixed.
sentences.mnemonic: abgemacht closes it. bis names the next time.
